findings.claim: The lessons call Hanako, Reiko and Etsuko the Hashimoto family.
findings.truth: They are the Tanaka family. The play's opening stage direction names the Tanaka household.
findings.evidence: Fetched Methuen play preview, pp. 9–10, lines 94–110

findings.claim: The play opens with Hanako and Reiko on the coast of Japan, arguing.
findings.truth: The opening is set at the Tanaka household during a storm; the Sea of Japan is present in the stage directions before the beach sequence.
findings.evidence: Fetched Methuen play preview, pp. 9–10, lines 94–110; Student Edition introduction, p. 13, lines 297–300

findings.claim: The play premiered at the Tricycle Theatre before transferring to the National Theatre's Dorfman.
findings.truth: Its world premiere was at the National Theatre's Dorfman on 19 March 2018, in a co-production with the Tricycle Theatre, now Kiln Theatre.
findings.evidence: Fetched Methuen play preview, p. 6, lines 47–68; National Theatre archive; Bloomsbury poster

findings.claim: Jung Sun is described with the pronoun 'He'.
findings.evidence: Fetched Methuen play preview, p. 9, lines 69–79; National Theatre cast record

findings.claim: Kum-Chol is the North Korean officer who oversees Hanako's captivity.
findings.truth: Kum-Chol becomes Hanako's husband in North Korea.
findings.evidence: Fetched contemporary production reviews and the National Theatre cast record; the reviews identify Kum-Chol as Hanako's husband

findings.claim: Turnly's grandfather was Japanese; he lived in Japan, speaks Japanese, and spent years researching with affected families.
findings.truth: Turnly's father met his Japanese mother while teaching English in Tokyo. Turnly reported six months of research; he said he had only restaurant-level Japanese and consulted language advisers.
findings.evidence: Fetched Guardian interview, lines 66–82, and National Theatre rehearsal diary

findings.claim: All the recognised Japanese abductions are described as being from coastal communities on Japan's western shore.
findings.truth: The 17 cases recognised by Japan occurred in Japan and overseas; the official list includes an abduction in Niigata city and cases in Europe as well as coastal disappearances.
findings.evidence: Japan Ministry of Foreign Affairs list of 17 recognised abductees

findings.claim: Japan in the 1980s was at the height of its economic miracle.
findings.truth: Japan experienced a major asset bubble in the late 1980s. Its collapse in the early 1990s preceded prolonged stagnation.
findings.evidence: Bank of Japan and IMF accounts of the late-1980s bubble and early-1990s stagnation

findings.claim: English stands in for Japanese while stylised Korean signals Hanako has been forced to learn a new language.
findings.truth: The play uses English alongside phonetic Japanese and Korean. Several scenes begin in Japanese or Korean before dialogue returns to English for the audience.
findings.evidence: Fetched Bloomsbury/National Theatre Student Edition description and contemporary production review

findings.claim: A gobo is a metal or glass plate placed in front of a lantern.
findings.truth: A gobo is a metal or glass patterned disc inserted in the gate of a profile lantern to project its pattern.
findings.evidence: Rosco technical documentation and Theatrecrafts lighting glossary

findings.claim: Across the unit, 12- and 20-mark tasks and exam tips present director-led intentions or multi-discipline staging responses as the board format.
findings.truth: AQA's Section B has 4-, 8-, 12- and 20-mark questions. AQA says the 12-mark item is a performer question, and the 20-mark items require a response as either a performer or for one chosen design skill. Options: retain these as explicitly house discursive tasks, or reframe all board-aligned tasks around the prescribed role choices.
findings.evidence: Specification 2.2 and 4.2.1; AQA Bringing Assessment to Life: Drama
findings.ruling: NOTE: AQA Drama Section B tasks are performer (12) / performer-or-one-design-skill (20); the unit frames director-led intentions tasks across lessons. Subject-wide relabel item for drama-aqa, not surgical.

findings.claim: The play is repeatedly classified as documentary theatre or documentary realism.
findings.truth: The published text states that all its names, characters and incidents are fictitious, while the publisher describes it as based on a true story. Options: describe it consistently as a fictional political play based on real abductions, or retain a documentary-theatre classification only with a sourced genre rationale. This affects lessons 1, 3, 4, 5 and 8.
findings.evidence: Fetched Methuen play preview, p. 9, lines 92–93; Bloomsbury Student Edition description
findings.ruling: NOTE: genre classification recurs in five lessons; the published text calls itself fictitious, publisher says based on a true story. Rebuild-level rewording; recorded for Tom.

findings.claim: The Pyongyang Declaration itself is called North Korea's first acknowledgement of the abductions.
findings.truth: At the September 2002 Japan–North Korea summit, Kim Jong-il admitted the abductions and apologised; the leaders also signed the Japan–DPRK Pyongyang Declaration. Options: distinguish the summit admission from the declaration throughout, or retain the shorthand only if its distinction is explained. The wording recurs in lessons 1, 4, 5 and 8.
findings.evidence: Japan Ministry of Foreign Affairs chronology and abductions overview
findings.ruling: NOTE: summit admission vs Pyongyang Declaration shorthand recurs in four lessons; low stakes at GCSE Drama; recorded.

findings.claim: Kum-Chol is broadly framed as a captor or complicit official after direct role references are corrected.
findings.truth: Available sources identify Kum-Chol as Hanako's husband and describe him as shaped by the regime. Options: retain the complicity reading as an explicitly arguable interpretation, or reframe the wider material around an enforced marriage and compromised survival. This would require coordinated changes in lessons 2, 3 and 8.
findings.evidence: Fetched National Theatre cast record and contemporary production reviews
findings.ruling: NOTE: Kum-Chol framing after the role fix is an arguable interpretation; left as read, recorded.

findings.claim: Several lessons say what examiners frequently note, reward, penalise or consider the most common error without identifying an examiner report.
findings.truth: No fetched AQA examiner report substantiated these recurring frequency claims. Treat them as house advice or supply a source; no isolated factual replacement is safe.
findings.evidence: AQA specification and fetched AQA assessment guidance

findings.claim: The lesson refers to a searchlight in the play's design history and says most productions use split staging.
findings.truth: The fetched original-production designer describes a sliding, revolving box and video design, not a permanent split stage or a documented searchlight motif. The lesson's alternatives are valid design proposals, but the production-history wording is unsupported.
findings.evidence: Fetched Tom Piper production-design account and National Theatre rehearsal diary

summary: Eight lessons were checked against the AQA specification, fetched publisher and National Theatre primary material, and reliable historical and technical sources. Thirty-seven surgical edits correct verified facts; three unit-wide issues need editorial adjudication.
